questions.prompt: Trace NetSlack's channel list and channel creation. Which channels does the list return and what does that rule leave open for the future? On create, how is the channel name normalized and checked against existing channels, what does the domain do with the creator, and what is the current rule for who may create a channel? Which test does the drill ask for?

keyPoints.text: The list returns public channels plus private channels the user has joined.
keyPoints.quote: Filters public or joined private channels

keyPoints.text: Future direct-message rules will need care in that filter.
The service trims the name, lower-cases it and replaces spaces with hyphens before checking it.
A channel with that normalized name already in the workspace is a conflict.
The domain creates the normalized channel and joins the creator to it.
keyPoints.quote: Creates normalized channel and joins creator

keyPoints.text: There is no role policy for creating channels: any workspace member may.
keyPoints.quote: Channel creation lacks role policy; current rule is "any workspace member".

keyPoints.text: Drill: a test proving a non-member cannot create a channel in another workspace.
keyPoints.quote: Write a test proving a non-member cannot create a channel in another workspace.

questions.prompt: Explain the message history read. What does the endpoint default take to and what does the service do with it, why is AsNoTracking used, how do OrderByDescending, Take and the final OrderBy combine (the drill), which index supports the read, what a real chat app would still need, and what the UI can briefly show while fetching.

keyPoints.text: The endpoint defaults take to 50.
The service checks access and clamps take to 1..100.
AsNoTracking matters for read-only queries.
OrderByDescending plus Take picks the newest N messages; the final OrderBy by PostedAt returns them oldest-first for display.
The (ChannelId, PostedAt) index supports the channel/time read.
A real chat app needs cursor pagination, a retention policy and a search strategy.
keyPoints.quote: A real chat app needs cursor pagination, retention policy, and search strategy.

keyPoints.text: The UI can briefly show the previous channel's messages during the fetch.
keyPoints.quote: State can briefly show old messages during fetch.

questions.prompt: How does a NetSlack user get a token, and what does development seeding do? Explain what the dev-token endpoint does with the request, what kind of authentication it is, how it is exposed and in which environments it is actually mapped, what is validated about the signing key, what the claims must stay aligned with, and how the seeder prepares the database and why that differs from migrations.

keyPoints.text: The dev-token endpoint creates or updates a user and returns a JWT.
keyPoints.quote: endpoint creates or updates a user and returns a JWT.

keyPoints.text: There is no password or OIDC: it is an intentional development shortcut.
The endpoint allows anonymous callers.
Its mapping is not wrapped in a Development check, so it is live in every environment, while seeding sits inside the IsDevelopment block.
The JWT signing key must be at least 32 characters.
The token's claims must match what CurrentUser reads.
The seeder calls EnsureCreated and skips seeding if any users exist.
EnsureCreated is not the same as migrations.
keyPoints.quote: `EnsureCreated` is not the same as migrations.
